post_text: People overcomplicate positioning. There are really just three strategies... Strategy 1: Position in a mature category against existing vendors You place yourself in an established category and argue why you're better than the competition. The upside: Customers already have budget for it, actively search for it, and don't need educating. The risk: Mature categories have big, entrenched players. Without serious differentiation and resources, you'll struggle to make the shortlist. Choose this if... • the category is large enough to meet your growth goals • you have the resources to compete head-to-head for the whole market • OR you're willing to focus an underserved subsegment Strategy 2: Take an existing (but small) category to a new audience You position in a known (but likely nascent) category and sell it to people who haven't heard of it yet. (E.g. Skrillex bringing Dubstep to the mainstream. DocuSign didn't invent e-signature, but they focused on selling it to companies that used paper. Dropbox didn't invent file sharing, but they popularized it.) The upside: • Less direct competition, more greenfield opportunity The risk: • You have to educate the market rather than waiting for inbound demand • You also inherit the category's reputation (for good or bad) Choose this if... • you believe the category will grow and you can become a leader as it solidifies • you have the marketing patience to play the long game Strategy 3: Create your own category You refuse to fit into anyone else's box and seek to build a new one. The upside: You get full control to define both the problem and solution framing. The risks: • you need to pick the right-sized problem (too broad and it's unbelievable) • first movers rarely win (Airbnb beat Vrbo, Google beat AltaVista), and large incumbents may simply copy your blueprint once you've proven the market, as Microsoft did to Slack. Choose this if... • you genuinely believe any existing category label would hurt more than help • you're prepared to invest years building awareness from scratch If you need help with your positioning, shoot me a DM and mention this post.

post_text: AI COMPANIES:Are your prospects asking "why should we use AI?"Or are they asking "why should we use YOUR AI?"There are two ways to message AI agent products:1) Assume your audience doesn't know what they are and isn't evaluating them, and you need to explain why they are worth looking intoThis makes sense in more immature ends of the market: legacy industries, highly regulated, slower moving industries, etc. There are still large portions of the enterprise that haven't jumped into the agent-adding frenzy. There are also individuals who are highly skeptical of AI as a concept (even if their only experience has been chatbots). They likely haven't gone deep into agents, and would need an explanation of what they are. This approach can be summed up in two words: WHY AI?If you're going after this more immature market segment, you need to answer WHY should someone adopt this new category they aren't familiar with? An example from Notion: "Notion agents capture knowledge, answer questions, and push projects forward — all while you sleep." This definition assumes someone doesn't know what AI agents are or how they work. This definition could apply to every other agent on the market. So it only makes sense for an audience that isn't aware of those other agents. But what if your audience DOES know about agents? Then you have approach number 2: 2) Assume your audience knows what agents are and is actively evaluating them or even using themThis other end of the market is more mature.They likely HAVE agents — or are on the verge of getting them. If you want to win this group, you don't have to explain WHY AI... they already know the why. Now you need to answer... why OUR ai? (I.e. what would make our AI different/better than the other ones being evaluated.) An example is Octonomy. They say: "The best AI platform for complex knowledge. 95% accuracy. No hallucinations." They are trying to show their differentiation against other AI agent vendors. Because they assume their audience IS mature, and knows the other agents exist. So they are trying to answer the question: "why should you choose OUR agents over the other ones you're evaluating."----------------If you're an AI company, think about your target market. Where are they in terms of adoption? And then evaluate your own homepage: Are you answering their core question?Or are you talking past them?
note: Framework de messaging de dos opciones (why AI vs why YOUR AI) con ejemplos nombrados (Notion, Octonomy). Convierte un concepto de positioning en post estructurado.

post_text: Your Product Managers may be silently destroying your ability to go-to-market effectively.Marty Cagan popularized the concept of four risks when creating a new product or feature: 1) value(will they buy it?)2) usability(can they use it?)3) feasibility(can we build it?)4) business viability(should we build it?)The fourth risk is often calculated... WITHOUT considering the impact on the product's existing positioning. Just because a MARKET for a feature exists, doesn't mean that your company can COMPETE in this market. So you can falsely come to the conclusion that a feature/feature-set passes the "viability" test, when in reality your business has no ability to win in that new market.But I find most product roadmap discussions miss this foundational truth all together! Nobody even realizes that supporting new use cases means entering completely new markets!Every use case has: → its own competitive alternatives→ its own required value framing→ its own demanded proof pointsJust because you CAN quickly spin up a new feature that solves a new use case... doesn't mean you SHOULD.And even though the product team SHOULD be highly connected to the GTM side of the business, it's just often not the case (especially in much larger orgs).
note: POV contrarian que liga positioning con producto (4 riesgos de Marty Cagan). Hook fuerte + 'casi nadie ve esto': enseñar provocando.

post_text: What actually IS an autonomous business? I started noticing the term 'autonomous business' when Amos Bar-Joseph entered RB2B's space and made a splash with an incredibly compelling narrative about AI and building the startup of the future. I remember reading posts from 2 years ago like it was yesterday… He had this exciting way of positioning himself as a true AI expert, creating a totally new type of startup. 'Just three guys and an army of 30 AI agents', 'scaling to $30m ARR' (my favorite credibility line ever). I - along with thousands of others - read these posts and WANTED all of these agents. But I also had this feeling that the way they were going about it, Swan AI wasn't ever going to be truly autonomous … Nor was that the goal. These guys were actually working around the clock with these agents, and planned to continue to do so indefinitely. And by the way - there is nothing wrong with that. In fact, I'd go as far as to say if you are NOT committed to working around the clock indefinitely, you will almost certainly NOT be successful. But back to my original question … Is 3 guys working around the clock ACTUALLY an autonomous business? My answer would be 'no'. I have a fairly un-evolved definition of an 'autonomous business' … My definition is 'a business that runs itself without any humans.' Ironically, when we started RB2B, that was the ultimate goal, but never became part of the story. We designed the entire machine to be simple enough to where all customer interaction could be handled by AI, and our cheap acquisition channel (my thought leadership) helped us price so low that people didn't expect more than that from us. Fast forward 2 years... We refuse to add anything beyond a pixel and a push, AI handles over 99% of our total customer tickets, and our CSAT is in the high 90's. What's even crazier is that we stopped working on RB2B six weeks ago to pursue MoltSets. What do I mean by that? - Tate has not touched the code in six weeks (true story) - Robb spends under 15min/day answering AI-escalated tickets - I post 3x/week on LinkedIn, ironically NOT about RB2B… And we're currently growing at over 7%/mo, will cross $10m ARR soon, and it's taking under 90min of human time per week. Based on my primitive definition - a business that runs itself w/o humans - RB2B is the closest thing to 'autonomous' that I've ever heard of. How would you define an autonomous business? What are other examples?

post_text: In 2017, a 45 minute podcast interview with Ross Andrew Paquette, where he said he bootstrapped to $25M ARR with only ONE sales rep, changed the trajectory of my life forever. BACKGROUND Have you ever heard of Roger Banister? In 1954, Roger Banister was the first human to run a mile under 4min. For 1000's of years, people believed that a human could not break 4min. Here's the crazy thing… By the end of 1955, 24 people had broken the 4min mile. Why? Because THEY NOW KNEW it was possible. This is the story of my Roger Banister moment. ACT 1 / ROBLY EMAIL MARKETING In 2014 I launched an Email Marketing app called Robly. We got stuck at $3m in 2016, and remained stuck until November 2019. ACT 2 / THE PODCAST Throughout the Robly journey, I was searching for any information that might get us unstuck. That's when I came across the podcast with Ross and learned he bootstrapped $25m ARR with ONE SALES REP! Insane! ACT 3 / THE GOAL Now I knew it was possible. And even though I was stuck at $235k MRR, $2MM MRR became my goal. I wrote in my journal that I would hit it by my 42nd birthday. ACT 4 / DIANA ROSSI I HAD to find out what Ross knew about the Email Marketing space that I didn't. So I hit up his old salespeople. That led to chatting with Diana Ross, who had left Maropost. We spoke more and more over the course of the year, and in 2018 decided to start a business together. ACT 5 / THE EPIC FAIL We spent a year building a new newsletter app, and our plan was to 'launch' at the Traffic & Conversions summit. At the event we collected some leads, but when I started talking with people I saw their reaction. All they were thinking was, 'How do I get this guy to stop talking to me?' I had to figure out how to salvage it. I remembered hearing it was possible to have an anonymous visitor hit a website and you could resolve it to an email address. I thought I could sell that to anybody. So on the second day of the trade show, I closed every conversation with: 'By the way, what if I could get you the email addresses of people who visited your website and didn't fill out a form?' BOOM!! People's eyes lit up. 'What did you just say???' Those conversations inspired the next 8 years of my life. ACT 6 / TODAY Those conversations led to GetEmails, which we launched on Nov 9, 2019. We didn't get to $25m with one rep, but… We DID get to $12m ARR with 6 people and only ONE REP! TAKEAWAY My life changed when I heard Ross got Maropost to $25m ARR with one rep. Startups can get WAY farther than you think, with FAR fewer resources. BUT... You must have YOUR OWN Roger Banister moment. YOU must realize what's possible. That's why this Tuesday, I'm sitting down LIVE with Ross Paquette himself. The man who inspired me is breaking down exactly how he scaled Maropost to $30M ARR, bought out his investors to reclaim total control, and built a $1.7B business on two metrics: Revenue and Profit. Join us for the live event.
